description: I am an Azerbaijani researcher and dedicated enthusiast of astrophysics and algorithms. Powered by a strong foundation in C++ and actively engaged in competitive programming, I focus on optimizing complex data structures and solving planetary computational problems with extreme efficiency at O(1) speed
summary:
High level summary of my amazing project:

What I developed:
I built Lunar Landing Site Navigator, a fast C++ tool and interactive browser timeline for lunar South Pole missions.

How it addresses the challenge:
Reading raw text tables from NASA JPL Horizons takes hours when launch dates change. My program parses this data in milliseconds, calculates the Moon's airless horizon dip, and shows exact sunlight hours and Earth signal windows on a clear visual graph.

Why it is important:
For Shackleton Crater, it found 100% sunlight (721 hours) and 41.75% Earth signal (301 hours). This lets engineers test backup landing dates fast and makes space data easy for anyone to understand.
details:
All of the details go here. Here are the details:

What my project does and how it works:

I built Lunar Landing Site Navigator to check sunlight hours and Direct-to-Earth communication windows near the Moon's South Pole. First, my C++ program (main.cpp) reads hourly Sun and Earth position files from NASA JPL Horizons, cleans the text, calculates the angles, and saves the results into a data.js file. Then, opening nasa.html in a browser shows that data on a 721-hour graph with a slider. For Shackleton Crater (Nov 14 to Dec 14, 2026), it found 721 hours of continuous sunlight (37.39 W/m² average solar power) and 301 hours where Earth is visible in the sky (41.75%).

What benefits it has:

It calculates a whole 30-day lunar cycle in less than 0.01 seconds. Because it only uses simple HTML and JavaScript files, it works offline in any browser without heavy software. You can move the slider to any hour and instantly see how much time is left until Sunset or Earthset.

What the intended impact is:

When rocket launches get delayed, engineers have to check new landing dates quickly. Instead of reading huge text tables by hand for hours, they can test new dates in seconds. Finding exact Direct-to-Earth windows also helps smaller landers send data home without needing expensive relay satellites. Students can also use the slider to easily see how the Sun and Earth move in the lunar sky.

What tools I used:

I used C++ for reading the files and doing the math, HTML5 Canvas and JavaScript for the chart and slider, and NASA JPL Horizons for the Sun and Earth data.

How my project is creative:

Instead of writing slow nested loops to find when the Sun or Earth sets at every hour, I wrote a single backwards loop so it finishes almost instantly. Having C++ directly create a data.js file also connects fast calculations to a browser page without needing a server.

What factors I considered:

Since the Moon has no atmosphere, light does not bend like on Earth, so I calculated the curved horizon dip (-0.0869 degrees for a 2-meter lander). I also factored in the low 1.5-degree sun angles at the South Pole using the 1361 W/m² solar constant, and the Moon's wobble that hides Earth below the horizon for about 60% of the month.
